summary: This unit teaches you to choose, check, use and look after power tools in a welding and fabrication shop, and to plan their safe use by a team. You will learn electrical safety, angle grinder discs and speeds, drilling speeds and magnetic drills, saws and nibblers, air tools and cordless batteries, and how to control noise, vibration, dust, fumes and fire. You will also learn the care a user may give a tool, what must go to a competent repairer, and how to tag faults, keep the register, supervise others and report incidents.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). Power tools (grinders, drills, magnetic drills, saws, nibblers, air tools and cordless tools) save hours of work, but they also cause many workshop injuries: discs that burst, tools that kick back, electric shocks, fires from sparks, hearing loss and damaged hands.

At Level 3 you do more than use the tools. You **choose** the right tool for each task, **plan** how a team will use them safely, **check** and **care** for them, **supervise** others, and keep the records that show every tool is safe.
**Who it is for:** Welding Level 3 trainees at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and anyone who leads a team that cuts, drills, grinds and finishes steel in the shop or on site.

What this means in the workshop
rows: Match the tool and its accessory to the material, the size of cut or hole, the number of parts and where the work is done.
Check the site and the supply, write a risk assessment, arrange permits, screens and PPE, and brief the team.
Tag and register, casing, guard, handle, switch, accessory, cable, plug, voltage and RCD.
Fit the right disc for the grinder's speed and size, keep the guard and side handle on, and avoid kickback.
Work out spindle speeds, clamp the work, use cutting fluid, and set up magnetic base drills correctly.
Set air pressure, look after hoses and the compressor; charge, store and handle lithium-ion batteries safely.
Noise, vibration, dust, fumes and fire, for the user and everyone nearby.
Clean and maintain tools as a user may, send repairs to a competent person, tag faults and keep the register.
Train and sign off new users, stop unsafe work, give toolbox talks and report incidents.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on choosing tools, electrical safety, grinders, drills and magnetic drills, air and cordless tools, health hazards, care, supervision and drill-speed sums.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms) and longer answers that explain how you would plan, check, use or care for power tools.

**Practical tasks**: as a team, plan and make a batch of steel brackets with power tools, with a risk assessment, tool check sheet and inspection sheet; and run an inspection and care session on the Centre's power tools and give a toolbox talk.

blocks.note: Short-answer questions ask for exact terms such as rpm (revolutions per minute), annular cutter, flap disc, bar, hand-arm vibration syndrome, chuck, carbon brushes, DO NOT USE, hot work permit, local exhaust ventilation, amp-hours and dead-man switch.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Choosing the tool and planning the job

blocks.p: The right tool makes the job safer, faster and better. Think about the material and its thickness, the size and accuracy of the cut or hole, how many parts there are, and where the work is done: in the shop or on site, how much space there is, what power is available, and what could catch fire or who could be hurt nearby.

Best tool
Why

Cold saw or bandsaw with a length stop
Square, repeatable cuts with little heat, burr or sparks

Fast and portable, but throws sparks
Cutting fixings next to timber or other things that burn
Reciprocating saw with a metal-cutting blade

No sparks and little distortion; stay within the rated thickness

blocks.p: Size matters too. A 115 or 125 mm grinder is light and easy to control for fine work and tight places. A 180 or 230 mm grinder is for heavy cuts in open spaces, and kicks back harder. Never force a big tool into a small space, or take a guard off to make it fit: use a smaller tool.

blocks.h: Planning safe use for a team

flow: Read the drawing and job card: materials, sizes, quantities, where the work is
Visit or ask about the site: power supply (110 V or 220 V, RCD protection, distance), space, things that burn, people nearby
Choose the tools and accessories; check they are available, tagged and in date
Write the risk assessment: each hazard and its controls
Arrange the hot work permit, screens, extinguisher and signs
Give each member tasks they are trained for
Brief the team before work starts

head: Hazard
Main controls
rows: Tools tagged and checked; RCD protection; leads rated and routed safely; no wet conditions
Right disc for the grinder; guard and side handle fitted; work clamped; correct technique
Safety glasses always; face shield for grinding and wire brushing; screens
Remove or cover things that burn; hot work permit; extinguisher; fire watch
Hearing protection for everyone in the area; quieter methods; signs
Low-vibration tools; time limits; task rotation
Extraction at the source; ventilation; respirators where needed
No loose clothing, jewellery or long hair near rotating parts
Cables and hoses along walls or under covers
Lift heavy sections and tools with help or lifting aids

blocks.note: Site jobs at schools, hotels and homes have members of the public, including children, close by. Mark off the work area, put up screens so sparks and arc light cannot reach them, and agree working times with the client.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Electrical safety and checks before use

ul: Jamaica's mains supply is **110 V and 220 V at 50 Hz**, and many workshops have both kinds of outlet. Check the voltage on the tool's **rating plate** before you plug in. A 110 V tool on 220 V burns out; a 220 V tool on 110 V runs weakly and overheats.
A tool made for a 60 Hz supply may behave differently on 50 Hz; check the plate says 50 Hz or 50/60 Hz.

**Current = power ÷ voltage.** A 2000 W tool on 220 V draws about 9 A; a 1100 W tool on 110 V draws 10 A. A 110 V tool draws twice the current of a 220 V tool of the same power, so it needs a heavier lead.

A **residual current device (RCD)** compares the current going out and coming back. If some leaks to earth, perhaps through you, it **cuts the power** in a fraction of a second. RCDs for tools usually trip at 30 mA; a GFCI outlet trips at a lower current (about 5 mA). They make a fatal shock much less likely, but they do not stop every shock.
Press the **test button** on a portable RCD before each use: it should trip at once. If it does not, do not use it.
**Class I** tools have a metal case connected to the earth pin of the plug. Never cut off or bend an earth pin.
**Class II** tools are **double insulated**: marked with a square inside a square, they need no earth wire.
Use an extension lead rated for at least the tool's current and the right voltage, in good condition, as short as practical and suitable for outdoor use on site.
A **drum lead must be fully unwound** when the current is near its rating: coiled cable cannot lose its heat and can melt. Many drums show two ratings, a lower one for when they are wound.
Do not plug one extension lead into another.
Keep plugs and sockets dry and off the ground.
Run cables **along walls, overhead or under cable covers**: never across walkways, through doorways, through puddles, or over hot metal and sharp edges.
Never carry a tool by its cable, or unplug it by pulling the cable.
On site generators, follow the maker's earthing instructions, use RCD protection, and keep fuel away from sparks and exhaust fumes out in the open air.
A **dead-man (hold-to-run) switch** must be held in for the tool to run and stops it when you let go.

A **lock-on button** keeps the switch on. Do not use it on hand-held grinding or cutting: if the power fails and comes back, a locked-on tool can **start by itself**. Some tools have restart protection, but do not rely on it.
Switch off and unplug a tool when the power fails, before changing an accessory, and when you leave it.

head: Check
What to look for
rows: Inspection and test tag in date; the tool is on the register
Cracks, missing screws, burn marks, blocked vents
Guard, side handle and other parts
Works freely and returns to off; any lock-on releases
Right type, size and speed rating for the tool and the job; undamaged; in date; fitted correctly
Cuts, kinks, burns, bare wires or taped joints; the outer sheath held firmly where it enters the tool and the plug
Cracks, bent or loose pins, burn marks, signs of heat
Voltage matches; RCD fitted and tested; lead rated and sound
Unusual noise, sparking, smell or vibration

blocks.note: If you find any fault, do not use the tool. Unplug it, tag it DO NOT USE, hand it in and report it. Never tape over a cut cable or repair a plug yourself: electrical repairs and tests are done by a competent person. A tool whose plug or lead gets hot in use has a poor connection or is overloaded: stop and have it checked.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Accessory
Used for
Points to know
rows: Cutting disc (thin and flat, about 1–3 mm)
Cutting bar, tube, angle and sheet
Cut with the edge only. **Never grind with the side**: side pressure can shatter a thin disc.
Removing weld caps, bevelling, heavy grinding
Hold it at a shallow angle to the work (often about 15–30°)
Blending and finishing welds, removing burrs, rounding corners
Coarse grits (about 40) remove metal; fine grits (about 120) finish; runs cooler and gouges less
Wire cup brush or wire wheel
Removing rust, paint, scale and slag
Wires break off and fly out: face shield over safety glasses, and covered skin
Iron-free discs, kept only for stainless, so carbon steel does not contaminate it

blocks.p: Every disc is marked with its **maximum speed** in rpm (revolutions per minute), and often with its maximum rim speed in metres per second. The disc's rpm rating must be **equal to or higher than** the no-load speed on the grinder's rating plate. A disc spun faster than its rating can burst, and the pieces fly out with enough force to kill.
The rim speed depends on both the rpm and the diameter: **rim speed (m/s) = π × diameter (mm) × rpm ÷ 60 000**.

head: Disc on an 11 000 rpm grinder
Rim speed
Result
rows: Below the 80 m/s rating of most bonded discs: safe
Far above its rating: it would burst

blocks.p: That is why a bigger disc must **never** be fitted to a smaller grinder, even with the guard removed. The disc's bore must also match the spindle and flanges.

Some grinders have a **variable speed** control, so the speed can suit the accessory and the work: lower speeds for flap discs, wire brushes and polishing, and for stainless steel to reduce heat. Never set it above the accessory's rating.

flow: Unplug the grinder (or take out the battery)
Check the disc: type, size, bore, speed rating, expiry date, and no cracks, chips or damp
Clean the flanges and fit them the right way round for that disc
Press the spindle lock only when the spindle is still, and tighten the nut with the key, not a hammer
Set the guard between the disc and you, so sparks and pieces go away from you
Stand to one side and run it at full speed for a short time (often about a minute for a new disc, as the maker says), pointed away from people
Stop if it wobbles or vibrates, and check the fitting

blocks.note: Resin-bonded discs weaken with age and damp, and many carry an expiry date, often on the metal centre ring. Scrap any disc that is past its date, has been dropped, has got wet, or is cracked or chipped. Store discs flat, in a dry place.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Hold it with **two hands**, with the side handle fitted on the side that suits the job.
Clamp the work or hold it in a vice: **never hold work in one hand** while you grind with the other.
Stand balanced, out of the line of the disc.
Let the disc reach full speed before it touches the work, and let the tool do the work: do not force it.
When cutting, keep the disc straight in the cut and do not twist it. Support long pieces so the cut opens as you go, rather than closing and pinching the disc.
Point the sparks away from people and from anything that can burn.
Never put the grinder down until the disc has stopped. Never remove the guard.

blocks.p: **Kickback** happens when the disc snags or is pinched in the cut: it stops suddenly and the grinder is thrown back towards the user, in a fraction of a second. Causes include a cut that closes on the disc, twisting the disc, cutting into a corner or sharp edge, the wrong disc, and a one-handed grip. Prevent it by supporting the work so the cut opens, keeping the disc straight, holding the grinder firmly with both hands, and standing to one side of the line of the disc. Never fit a toothed wood-cutting blade to an angle grinder.

sections.title: Drills, magnetic drills and drilling speeds

ul: The **chuck** grips the drill bit. Take the **chuck key** out before you switch on: a key left in the chuck is thrown out.
Use high-speed steel (HSS) twist drills for steel, and cobalt HSS drills for stainless and harder steels. The usual point angle is about 118°.
Centre-punch the hole position so the drill starts in the right place.
For large holes, drill a **pilot hole** first, a little larger than the web (the chisel edge) of the big drill.
**Clamp the work.** Never hold small parts or thin sheet by hand: as the drill breaks through, it can grab the work and spin it round.
Ease off the feed as the drill breaks through. Clamp thin sheet to a backing board, or use a step drill.

blocks.note: At a pillar drill, tie back long hair and keep sleeves, jewellery and cloths away from the chuck and drill. Gloves can be caught by a turning chuck or drill and pull your hand in: follow the Centre's rule, which often bans gloves at the pillar drill. Clear swarf with a brush or hook, never your fingers.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: The **cutting speed (V)** is how fast the cutting edge moves past the metal, in metres per minute. It depends on the material being drilled and the drill material. The **spindle speed (N)** in rpm is then:

blocks.note: N = (1000 × V) ÷ (π × D), where D is the drill diameter in millimetres.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Material
Typical cutting speed for HSS drills (m/min)

blocks.p: These are typical figures: follow the drill maker's chart.

**Worked example:** a 14 mm HSS drill in mild steel at 25 m/min. N = (1000 × 25) ÷ (3.142 × 14) = 25 000 ÷ 44.0 ≈ 568 rpm. If the drill's speeds are 330, 520 and 780 rpm, choose **520 rpm**, the nearest speed below the answer.

ul: A **bigger drill runs slower**, because its edge travels further in each turn.
**Too fast:** the drill overheats, its edges burn and go blunt, and stainless steel work-hardens.
**Too slow:** cutting is slow, and heavy feed can chip or break the drill.
Keep a **steady, firm feed**. A light, rubbing feed lets stainless steel **work-harden**, and then it is very hard to cut.
Use cutting fluid as the maker says: usually soluble oil or cutting paste on steel and stainless; cast iron and brass are often drilled dry.

blocks.p: A **magnetic base drill** holds itself to steel with an electromagnet. It usually drives an **annular cutter**: a hollow cutter that cuts only a ring of metal and leaves a solid core, the **slug**. It cuts large holes faster and with less power than a twist drill. A spring-loaded **pilot pin** in the middle centres the cutter and pushes the slug out at the end.

flow: Check the drill's tag, cable and switch; choose a sharp annular cutter of the right size and depth, with its pilot pin
Clean the steel where the magnet will sit: no paint, scale, rust, swarf or grease; flat; at least the maker's minimum thickness
Mark and punch the hole centre; line the pilot pin up on the punch mark
Switch the magnet on and check it holds firmly
Fit the safety strap or chain round the beam, especially on upright or overhead faces
Make sure nobody is welding on that steel, and nobody is under an overhead cut
Fill the coolant bottle; wear safety glasses and hearing protection
Start the motor, feed in gently, then with steady pressure, letting the swarf clear
After breakthrough, retract the cutter, switch off the motor and wait for it to stop
Hold the drill, then switch off the magnet
Remove the slug and swarf with a hook or pliers: they are hot and sharp

ul: The magnet holds much less well on thin plate, paint, scale or uneven steel. If the power fails, the magnet lets go: the safety strap stops the drill falling or spinning round.
Never use a magnetic drill on steel that is being arc welded: the welding current can flow through the drill and its magnet, damaging them and its earth lead.
Blue swarf, smoke or squealing mean the cutter is running hot: check the cutting fluid is reaching it, and the speed and feed.

sections.title: Saws, nibblers and other power tools

head: Tool
Used for
Safety and care
rows: Square, accurate cuts in bar, tube and sections
Clamp in the vice; length stop; guard down; coolant; blade pitch to suit the section
Cutting bar and sections, many pieces; shapes on a vertical saw
Blade tension and tracking set; guides close to the work; at least three teeth in the section; coolant
Disc rated for the saw; guard; work clamped; sparks away from people; burrs and hot ends
Cutting fixings in place, demolition, near timber
Few sparks; firm grip; check for hidden cables and pipes
Fine-tooth metal blade; sheet clamped and supported
Curves and openings in sheet within its rated thickness
Start from a drilled hole; little distortion; sharp, crescent-shaped swarf
Straight cuts and gentle curves in sheet
Within its rated thickness; keep fingers clear of the blades
Small grinding jobs in tight places, deburring
Very high speed: burrs and points rated for it; eye protection
Removing scale, rust, slag and old paint
Strong vibration and noise: limit time; hearing protection
Impact-rated sockets only; check the final torque with a torque wrench where the job asks
Tool rest close to the wheel (the maker's gap, often about 2–3 mm); eye shield and guards fitted; do not grind on the side of a straight wheel; not for aluminium, which clogs the wheel

ul: Keep **at least three teeth** in contact with the section, or the teeth snag and break.
Use a finer pitch (more teeth) for thin walls and sheet, and a coarser pitch for thick solid bar.
Use coolant where the saw has it: it keeps the blade sharp and the cut cool.

blocks.note: A cold saw or bandsaw makes no sparks and gives square, repeatable cuts, so for a batch of the same length it is usually safer and better than an abrasive disc.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Compressed air is **stored energy**. It is measured in **bar** (and in psi on some gauges: 1 bar ≈ 14.5 psi). Many air tools are rated about 6–6.3 bar (about 90 psi) at the tool, while the receiver may hold 8–10 bar. Set the **regulator** to the pressure the tool maker gives: too much pressure can make a tool or its accessory over-speed and fail.

head: Hazard
Control
rows: A hose that parts whips and strikes people
Check couplings and hoses; fit whip checks (safety cables) across joints; replace a bulging, cut or worn hose
Air forced into skin, eyes or ears
Never point air at anyone; never blow dust off clothes or skin; use a brush or vacuum
Regulator set to the tool's rating
Shut off the air, bleed the line and disconnect the tool before changing a cutter or clearing a jam
Hearing protection; task rotation; low-vibration tools
Hoses along walls or overhead; coiled away after use

ul: Water condenses in the receiver and lines. **Drain the receiver and the filters daily** (or as the maker says), or tools rust inside and run slowly.

A filter, regulator and lubricator unit (FRL) cleans the air, sets the pressure and, where the tool needs it, adds oil. Oil tools as the maker says: some need a few drops each day, some must not be oiled.
Check the compressor's safety valve, belt guard and oil, and have the receiver inspected as required.

blocks.note: Jamaica's humid air puts a lot of water into compressed air systems. Drain the receiver every day, especially in the rainy seasons.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: The **voltage** (for example 18 V) is the battery's power class. The **amp-hours (Ah)** show how much charge it stores. An 18 V 5.0 Ah battery stores 2½ times as much as an 18 V 2.0 Ah one, so it runs the tool about 2½ times as long, but it is heavier. Energy in watt-hours = volts × amp-hours: 18 × 5.0 = 90 Wh.
**Take the battery out** before changing a bit, blade or disc, clearing a jam, or putting the tool away.

Charge only on the **maker's charger**, on a hard surface that will not burn, in a cool, dry, ventilated place away from anything that burns. Let a hot battery cool before charging, and do not leave batteries charging unattended for long where the Centre's rules forbid it.
Protect the terminals. Keep batteries away from nails, screws, coins and other loose metal that can **short** them: a shorted battery can overheat and catch fire.
Keep batteries out of the sun, off hot steel and out of hot vehicles.

A battery that has been dropped hard, or is **swollen, cracked, leaking, very hot or smells**, is taken out of use at once, kept away from anything that burns, reported, and disposed of through the approved route, never in the ordinary bin. Lithium-ion fires are hard to put out and can flare up again.
For long storage, keep batteries in a cool, dry place, part-charged as the maker says.

blocks.note: Never open, repair or modify a battery, and use only the batteries and chargers the maker approves for the tool.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Grinders, cut-off saws, needle scalers and air chisels are very loud. Hearing damage builds up over months and years **without pain**, and it is permanent. Ringing in the ears (tinnitus) is a warning sign.
**Everyone in the noisy area** wears hearing protection, not only the person using the tool. Put up signs.
Ear plugs must be fitted properly; muffs must seal round the ear. Cotton wool does not protect.
Use quieter methods and tools, and keep noisy work away from others.

blocks.p: Long use of vibrating tools can cause **hand-arm vibration syndrome (HAVS)**: tingling and numbness in the fingers, fingers that go **white** (blanching), pain, and loss of grip and feeling. It can also cause carpal tunnel syndrome. If ignored, the damage becomes permanent. Needle scalers, chipping hammers, grinders and impact wrenches are the worst.

head: Control
Example
rows: Cut with a cold saw instead of grinding; clean steel by blasting instead of needle scaling
Tools and handles designed to reduce vibration
Sharp, balanced discs and cutters vibrate less and cut faster
No one uses a vibrating tool all day; regular breaks
Grip no tighter than needed; let the tool do the work
Report tingling, numbness or white fingers early; health checks

ul: Grinding and cutting throw out fine metal dust.
Cutting or grinding **galvanised** steel gives off zinc fume, which causes **metal fume fever** (flu-like chills and fever). Old paint may contain **lead**, which is poisonous.
Cutting concrete or masonry gives off silica dust, which damages the lungs.

Control dust and fumes at the source with **local exhaust ventilation (LEV)**, a hood and fan close to where they are made. Work in a well-ventilated area, and wear a suitable respirator where the risk assessment says. Wash before eating or drinking.
Grinding and cutting sparks can fly 10 metres or more and smoulder in timber, rags, dust or dry grass for a long time before flaring up.
Where there is a fire risk, a **hot work permit** is often needed before using a grinder or other spark-making tool.
Remove what can burn, or cover it with fire-resistant blankets; use screens; keep an extinguisher at hand; keep a fire watch during and after the work, as the permit says.
Never grind or cut near fuel, gas cylinders, or tanks and drums that held fuel.

head: Hazard
PPE
rows: Safety glasses at all times; a face shield over them for grinding, cutting and wire brushing
Leather gloves (but see the rule for the pillar drill)
Flame-resistant cotton clothing, sleeves down; leather apron; no synthetic fabrics
Respirator, as the risk assessment says

blocks.note: PPE is the last line of defence. Guards, clamps, extraction, safe methods and keeping people away come first; PPE protects you when something gets past them.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: What the user may do, and what needs a competent repairer

head: The user may
Only a competent repairer may
rows: Keep the tool clean; brush or blow out the vents with eye protection on
Check that screws, guards and handles are tight
Change discs, bits and blades, and keep them sharp
Oil the tool as the maker says
Replace a damaged cable or plug
Replace carbon brushes, switches or bearings
Do the electrical safety test after a repair

head: Sign
Likely cause
rows: Heavy sparking inside the vents and loss of power
Worn **carbon brushes** (the small carbon blocks that carry current to the motor's spinning part) or a worn commutator
Bent spindle, damaged or badly fitted disc

flow: Stop and unplug it (or take out the battery)
Tag it DO NOT USE
Take it out of service to the store
Fill in a fault report: date, tool number, what is wrong, who found it
Update the register
Competent person repairs and tests it
The repair and test are recorded
Only then does it go back into service

ul: The **register** lists every tool: its number, type, serial number, where it is kept, its inspection and test dates and results, the next date due, and its repairs.
The **tag** on the tool shows when it was last inspected and tested, when it is next due, and by whom.
The Centre sets how often tools are inspected and tested; tools used on site or in hard conditions are usually checked more often.
The register shows that each tool has been checked and is safe, gives its history, and helps plan replacements.
Keep tools in a **clean, dry, locked store**. Humid, salty air causes rust and electrical faults.
Keep tools in their cases. Coil cables loosely; do not wind them tightly round the tool, which strains the cable where it enters.
Store discs flat in a dry place, and keep batteries apart from loose metal.
Sign tools out and back in, so you know where each one is.
**Train and sign off** each person before they use a tool on their own: show them, watch them use it, then sign their competence record.
**Stop unsafe work at once**, put it right and explain why: for example a grinder used without its side handle, a guard removed, or work held by hand.
Give **toolbox talks** on tool hazards: short, practical, with the tool in hand.
At the end of the day, check each tool is clean, undamaged and logged back in, and that faults are reported.
Follow the rules yourself: the team copies what you do, not what you say.

flow: Make the area safe: switch off and unplug the tool, keep others away
Give first aid or call the first aider; call an ambulance if needed (110 in Jamaica)
Leave the tool, the broken pieces and the area as they are, as far as is safe
Tag the tool out of use
Report to the supervisor at once
Write the incident report

blocks.p: The incident report gives: the date, time and place; who was involved and any witnesses; what they were doing; the injury and the first aid given; the tool's number, the accessory's type, size and speed rating, and whether the guard and side handle were fitted; the likely cause; and actions to stop it happening again, such as disc checks, training or a toolbox talk.
Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise with your instructor.

ul: I can choose the best power tool and accessory for a cutting, drilling, grinding or finishing job.
I can plan a team's safe use of power tools, with a risk assessment and the right permits and controls.
I can check a tool, its lead and the supply before use, and explain tags and the register.
I can explain RCDs, Class I and Class II tools, and why the voltage must match the rating plate.
I can work out the current a tool draws and choose a suitable extension lead.
I can choose a grinder disc, check its speed rating, fit it and set the guard.
I can work out a disc's rim speed and explain why a big disc must never go on a small grinder.
I can use a grinder with two hands, with the work clamped, and explain how to avoid kickback.
I can work out a drill's spindle speed with N = (1000 × V) ÷ (π × D) and choose a machine speed.
I can set up and use a magnetic base drill safely.
I can choose and use saws, nibblers, shears and other power tools for the right jobs.
I can set air pressure, look after hoses and the compressor, and use air tools safely.
I can charge, store and handle lithium-ion batteries, and deal with a damaged one.
I can control noise, vibration, dust, fumes and fire, and choose the right PPE.
I can carry out user care and know what must go to a competent repairer.
I can tag and report a faulty tool and keep the register up to date.
I can train and supervise others, give a toolbox talk, and write an incident report.

A grinder disc made of overlapping abrasive leaves, for blending and finishing
Hand-arm vibration syndrome: damage to the hands from long use of vibrating tools
A written permit needed before work that makes sparks or heat where there is a fire risk
A tool being thrown back at the user when its disc or blade snags
Local exhaust ventilation: a hood and fan that remove dust and fumes at the source
A button that holds a tool's switch on
A drill that holds itself to steel with an electromagnet
The pin in an annular cutter that centres it and pushes out the slug
Residual current device: cuts the power fast when current leaks to earth
The valve that sets the air pressure delivered to a tool
How fast the edge of a disc travels, in metres per second
The button that holds a grinder's spindle while the disc is changed
The record of every tool, its tests, faults and repairs
A safety cable across an air hose coupling that stops the hose lashing if it parts
Metal, such as stainless steel, getting harder when it is rubbed or worked

c1.title: Hurricane-shutter brackets at a guest house in Treasure Beach
c1.text: Shernette leads a small team replacing rusted steel hurricane-shutter brackets on the timber walls of a guest house in Treasure Beach, St Elizabeth. The old brackets are fixed to the wooden window frames with steel lugs. The house has 110 V and 220 V outlets. The team has a 2200 W, 220 V angle grinder, a reciprocating saw, a portable RCD, and a 25 m drum extension lead labelled 13 A unwound and 5 A fully wound.

c2.title: Drilling beams at a packing house in Port Antonio
c2.text: Garth's team is fitting new steel beams in a banana packing-house extension in Port Antonio, Portland. Holes of 18 mm must be cut through the 10 mm flanges of beams already in place overhead, using a magnetic base drill with annular cutters. Loose connection plates need 16 mm holes, drilled with HSS twist drills on a pillar drill whose speeds are 280, 450, 700 and 1100 rpm. The plates are mild steel, and the cutting speed used is 25 m/min.

c3.title: Air tools in a truck-body shop in Linstead
c3.text: A truck-body shop in Linstead, St Catherine, runs its air tools from a compressor whose receiver is set at 10 bar. Its die grinders are rated 6.2 bar. Water spits out of the hoses when they are first connected, and the tools have been running slowly. Sheldon has used a needle scaler on old chassis rails for most of every day this week, and says his fingers tingle and go numb at night. One hose has a bulge near a coupling.

c4.title: The cordless tool store in Brown's Town
c4.text: At a training centre in Brown's Town, St Ann, the cordless drills and grinders use 18 V batteries of 2.0 Ah and 5.0 Ah. The chargers stand on a wooden shelf in a small, hot storeroom with no ventilation. Spare batteries are kept loose in a box of screws and nails.

c5.title: A new trainee on the grinder in Annotto Bay
c5.text: Kadeem, a new trainee at a training centre in Annotto Bay, St Mary, is learning to use a 125 mm angle grinder with a no-load speed of 11 000 rpm. The discs in the store are marked 80 m/s. To flatten a weld, Kadeem starts grinding with the side of a thin cutting disc, and he holds small pieces in one hand while he grinds them with the other.

questions.q: Which tool will cut the steel lugs next to the wooden frames with the fewest sparks?
o: The angle grinder with a thin cutting disc
The angle grinder with a grinding disc fitted
An abrasive cut-off saw set up on the ground below
A reciprocating saw with a metal-cutting blade
questions.why: A reciprocating saw cuts steel with teeth and throws very few sparks, so it suits work right next to timber. Abrasive discs throw showers of sparks that can lodge and smoulder in the wood.

questions.q: About how much current does the 2200 W, 220 V grinder draw?
o: About 2 A
About 5 A
About 10 A
About 20 A
questions.why: Current = power ÷ voltage = 2200 ÷ 220 = 10 A. The lead must be rated for at least that much current.

questions.q: How should the drum lead be used with this grinder?
o: Half unwound, which is plenty for a single grinder
Wound up, so that the cable stays tidy on site
Any way at all, since 10 A is below its 13 A rating
Fully unwound, as 10 A is above its wound rating
questions.why: Coiled cable cannot lose heat, which is why the drum is rated only 5 A when wound. With 10 A flowing it must be fully unwound, or the cable can overheat and melt.

questions.q: How should Shernette check the portable RCD before work starts?
o: Plug the grinder in and watch for the light
Press its test button and see that it trips
Check that its cable is long enough for the job
Switch it on and off a few times at the socket
questions.why: The test button makes a small leak on purpose, and a working RCD trips at once. If it does not trip, it gives no protection and must not be used.

questions.q: Why must nobody stand under the magnetic drill while it cuts through an overhead flange?
o: The magnet may let go as soon as the cutter starts
Coolant runs down on them and makes the floor slippery
The pilot pin pushes out the hot, sharp slug
Swarf from the cutter is thrown straight down in a shower
questions.why: An annular cutter leaves a solid slug, and the spring-loaded pilot pin ejects it as the cutter breaks through. Overhead, it drops hot and sharp onto anyone below.

questions.q: Which pillar drill speed should be used for the 16 mm holes in the plates?
o: 280 rpm
450 rpm
700 rpm
1100 rpm
questions.why: N = (1000 × 25) ÷ (3.142 × 16) = 25 000 ÷ 50.3 ≈ 497 rpm. Choose the nearest speed below that figure, 450 rpm; 700 rpm would overheat the drill.

questions.q: Partway through a hole, the magnetic drill's swarf turns blue and the cutter squeals. What should the operator check first?
o: That the cutting fluid is reaching the cutter
That the safety strap is pulled up tight
That the drill is plugged into a 110 V outlet
That the magnet switch is turned fully on
questions.why: Blue swarf and squealing mean the cutter is overheating. Without coolant the teeth soften and blunt quickly; check the fluid flow, then the speed and the feed.

questions.q: After the cutter breaks through, in what order should the operator stop the drill?
o: Magnet off first, then stop the motor while it is still cutting
Stop the motor, then switch off the magnet and let the drill drop
Retract, stop the motor, hold the drill, then magnet off
Leave the motor running and switch off the magnet to remove it
questions.why: Retract and stop the cutter first, then hold the drill before the magnet is released, so it cannot fall or swing. The safety strap is the back-up, not the plan.

questions.q: What should be done about the air pressure for the die grinders?
o: Leave it at 10 bar so the tools run faster
Lower the receiver to 5 bar for every tool
Raise it to 12 bar to make up for the water
Set the regulator to the tools' 6.2 bar
questions.why: Air tools are rated for a set pressure, and too much can make them or their accessories over-speed and fail. The regulator sets the pressure at the tool; the receiver can stay higher.

questions.q: What is the most likely cure for the water in the hoses and the slow-running tools?
o: Drain the receiver and the filters every day
Oil the tools twice as often as the maker says
Fit longer hoses so the water has time to dry
Turn the receiver pressure up to blow the water out
questions.why: Water condenses in the receiver and lines, especially in humid weather, and rusts tools inside. Draining the receiver and filters daily removes it.

questions.q: What should the team leader do about Sheldon's symptoms?
o: Give him thicker gloves and let him carry on as before
Wait to see whether the numbness goes after the weekend
Treat them as early signs of HAVS: rotate his work and report it
Tell him to grip the needle scaler more tightly to cut the shaking
questions.why: Tingling and numbness after long use of a vibrating tool are early signs of hand-arm vibration syndrome. Cutting his exposure, rotating tasks and getting a health check stop it becoming permanent.

questions.q: One hose has a bulge near a coupling. What should be done with it?
o: Take it out of use and replace it
Wrap the bulge tightly with tape
Use it only at a lower pressure
Move it to a tool that uses less air
questions.why: A bulge shows the hose wall is failing, and it can burst and whip. A damaged hose is replaced; tape or lower pressure does not make it safe.

questions.q: On the same 18 V drill, how does the 5.0 Ah battery compare with the 2.0 Ah one?
o: It makes the drill turn about 2½ times faster
It charges about 2½ times faster
It gives exactly the same running time
It runs the drill about 2½ times as long
questions.why: Amp-hours measure how much charge the battery stores. At the same voltage, 5.0 Ah runs the tool about 2½ times as long as 2.0 Ah; the speed and power stay much the same.

questions.q: Why should the spare batteries not be kept loose in the box of screws and nails?
o: The metal can scratch the battery labels
The batteries go flat faster near steel
Metal can short them and start a fire
The screws pick up a magnetic charge
questions.why: Loose metal across the terminals makes a short circuit, and a shorted lithium-ion battery can overheat and catch fire. Keep terminals covered and batteries apart from loose metal.

questions.q: Which change to the charging set-up is needed?
o: Keep the door shut so that dust cannot reach the chargers
Charge every battery overnight so they are always full
Cover the chargers with a cloth so dust cannot get into them
Move them to a cool, airy spot on a surface that cannot burn
questions.why: Heat and poor ventilation raise the risk of a battery fire, and a wooden shelf can burn. Charge on the maker's charger on a non-combustible surface, in a cool, dry, ventilated place.

questions.q: About how fast is the rim of a 125 mm disc moving on this grinder?
o: About 36 m/s
About 72 m/s
About 144 m/s
About 4320 m/s
questions.why: Rim speed = π × 125 × 11 000 ÷ 60 000 ≈ 72 m/s, which is within the discs' 80 m/s rating. Using the radius instead of the diameter would give the wrong figure of 36 m/s.

questions.q: What should the instructor do when Kadeem grinds with the side of the cutting disc?
o: Let him go on, but at a lower speed
Show him how to press harder evenly
Stop him: side pressure can shatter it
Tell him to turn the disc over halfway
questions.why: Thin cutting discs are made to take load on their edge only, and side pressure can break them apart. A grinding disc or flap disc is the right accessory for flattening a weld.

questions.q: What should Kadeem do with the small pieces he is grinding?
o: Hold them in a leather glove instead
Hold them with pliers in his other hand
Rest them on his knee to steady them
Clamp them in a vice or to the bench
questions.why: Small pieces held by hand can be snatched by the disc, and the hand is close to it. Clamping frees both hands for the grinder, which also needs two-handed control.

questions.q: Kadeem has just fitted a new disc. What should he do before using it on the work?
o: Tap the disc with a spanner and listen for a clear ring
Run it at full speed briefly, standing to one side
Press it hard against scrap to bed it in at once
Take the guard off to check the disc is centred
questions.why: A short run at full speed with the guard on, the disc pointed away from people and the user standing aside, shows up a faulty or badly fitted disc before it touches the work.

questions.q: A drill's rating plate shows a square inside a square. What does this mean?
o: It is double insulated and needs no earth
It must be earthed through a three-pin plug
It is only for use on a 110 V supply
It has passed its yearly electrical test
questions.why: The double square marks a Class II, double-insulated tool, protected by two layers of insulation instead of an earth wire. It still needs its checks before use and its test tag.
